## Today's topics

-   Count data
-   Example and theory
-   Overdispersion and quasi-likelihood
-   Gamma regression
-   Multinomial regression

## Example - Student arrivals

Number of students coming in the last minute before the lecture so far
in the course:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
students <- c(2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 5, 3, 1)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=6}
barplot(table(factor(students, levels=0:max(students))), 
        ylab="Frequency", xlab="Number of students", main="Histogram of student arrivals",
        col="lightgray")
```

## Count response

$$
Y \in [0,1,\ldots \infty )
$$ for $i = 1,\ldots, n$

We assume

$$Y \sim Poisson(\lambda)$$

Further, theory says:

$$\mu = E(Y) = \lambda>0$$ $$\sigma^2 = Var(Y) = \lambda >0$$

## Poisson probability model

The probability mass function mapping the probability of exactly $k$
events is given by:

$$ P(Y = k) = \frac{\lambda^k \exp(-\lambda)}{k!} $$

## Estimating the Poisson parameter

For the student arrivals data, we can estimate the parameter $\lambda$
using the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE), which is the sample mean.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# MLE of Poisson parameter lambda is the sample mean
lambda_hat <- mean(students)
lambda_hat
```

**So for students** $\lambda = 2$:

\- No-one late ($k=0$):
$P(Y=0) = \frac{2^0 \exp(-2)}{0!} = e^{-2} \approx 0.135$

\- Two late ($k=2$):
$P(Y=2) = \frac{2^2 \exp(-2)}{2!} = 2e^{-2} \approx 0.271$

## Shapes of the Poisson distribution

The shape of the Poisson PMF changes directly with $\lambda$. Here we
also overlay $\lambda=2$ representing our student arrivals data.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=6}
x_vals <- 0:15
plot(x_vals, dpois(x_vals, 1), type="b", col="red", pch=16, 
     ylab="Probability", xlab="y", main="Poisson PMF for different lambda")
lines(x_vals, dpois(x_vals, 2), type="b", col="black", pch=15, lwd=2)
lines(x_vals, dpois(x_vals, 4), type="b", col="blue", pch=17)
lines(x_vals, dpois(x_vals, 10), type="b", col="green3", pch=18)
legend("topright", legend=c(expression(lambda==1), expression(lambda==2~" (Students)"), expression(lambda==4), expression(lambda==10)), 
       col=c("red", "black", "blue", "green3"), pch=c(16, 15, 17, 18), lty=1, lwd=c(1, 2, 1, 1))
```

## The log-link function

The canonical link function for Poisson distributed response is the
`log`-link.

Hence we assume that the linear predictor

$\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$ is related
to the mean through the link function:

$$g(\lambda_i) = \log(\lambda_i)$$

by:

$$\log(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$$

Since we want:

$${\lambda}_i = \exp({\beta}_0 + {\beta}_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + {\beta}_p x_{pi}) > 0$$

## The inverse link-function

The inverse link function $\exp()$ provides the estimates of the mean
from estimated regression coefficients:

$$\widehat{\lambda}_i = \exp(\widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \widehat{\beta}_p x_{pi})$$

## Example - Plant Species

Number of plant species in plots of different biomass and pH.

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(BIAS.data)
data(species)
head(species, 4)
```

## Example - Plant Species (Cont.)

Number of plant species in plots of different biomass and pH.

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(BIAS.data)
data(species)
attach(species)
plot(Biomass,Species,type="n")
spp<-split(Species,pH)
bio<-split(Biomass,pH)
points(bio[[1]],spp[[1]],pch=16, col="red")
points(bio[[2]],spp[[2]],pch=16,col="green")
points(bio[[3]],spp[[3]],pch=16,col="blue")
legend(x="topright", legend=c("high", "medium", "low"), pch=16,
       col=c("red", "blue", "green"), title="pH")
```

## Species count as function of biomass

A Poisson regression with `Biomass` as predictor:

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
mod1.glm <- glm(Species ~ Biomass, family=poisson(log), data=species)
summary(mod1.glm)
```

## Output {.smaller}

A Poisson regression with `Biomass` as predictor:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
mod1.glm <- glm(Species ~ Biomass, family=poisson(log), data=species)
summary(mod1.glm)
```

## Deviance test for the effect of biomass

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
library(mixlm)
anova(mod1.glm,test='LR')
```

## Output

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(mixlm)
anova(mod1.glm,test='LR')
```

Conclusion: Biomass is highly significant with a negative effect on
species count.

## Delta unit interpretation

Using a log-link makes the interpretation of the slope
**multiplicative**. This is easy to derive:

$$ \color{blue}{\log(\mu_{\text{new}})} - \color{blue}{\log(\mu_{\text{old}})} = (\beta_0 + \beta_1(x+1)) - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) = \color{red}{\beta_1} $$
$$ \implies \log\left(\frac{\mu_{\text{new}}}{\mu_{\text{old}}}\right) = \color{red}{\beta_1} \implies \mu_{\text{new}} = \mu_{\text{old}} \color{red}{\exp(\beta_1)} $$

Taking a 1-unit delta (increase) in predictor $x_j$ **multiplies** the
expected **mean** response **by** $\exp(\beta_j)$.

For example, $\widehat{\beta}_{\text{Biomass}} = -0.0644$. A 1-unit
increase in `Biomass` multiplies the expected species count by
$\exp(-0.0644) \approx 0.938$, which corresponds to a decrease of
$6.2\%$.

## Prediction

What is the predicted species count for a plot with biomass equal to 4?

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
new <- data.frame(Biomass=4)
    link <- predict(mod1.glm, new, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
    response <- predict(mod1.glm, new, type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
    LS <- cbind(link$fit, link$se.fit, response$fit, response$se.fit)
    colnames(LS) <- c("link", "se.link", "response", "se.response")
    LS
```

## Output

```{r, echo=FALSE}
new <- data.frame(Biomass=4)
    link <- predict(mod1.glm, new, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
    response <- predict(mod1.glm, new, type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
    LS <- cbind(link$fit, link$se.fit, response$fit, response$se.fit)
    colnames(LS) <- c("link", "se.link", "response", "se.response")
    LS
```

This was found by letting $x^{*} = 4$ and

$$\widehat{\eta}^{*} = 3.184 - 0.0644\cdot x^{*} = 2.926$$

$$\widehat{y}^{*} = \widehat{\lambda}^{*} = \exp(\widehat{\eta}^{*}) = \exp(2.926) = 18.66$$

## Expanding the model

From the plot we saw that `pH` may have large influence.

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
mod2.glm <- glm(Species ~ Biomass + pH, family=poisson, data=species)
summary(mod2.glm)
```

## Output (Expanded model) {.smaller}

From the plot we saw that `pH` may have large influence.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
mod2.glm <- glm(Species ~ Biomass + pH, family=poisson, data=species)
summary(mod2.glm)
```

## Deviance tests

```{r, echo=TRUE}
anova(mod2.glm,test='LR')
```

## Over/under-dispersion

$Var(y)$ depends on the mean $\mu$ in specific ways for the binomial and
the Poisson distribution (and others).

Sometimes data vary more (over-dispersion) or less (under-dispersion)
than expected.

Over-dispersion is very common in biological data

Usually this is due to some (unknown) factor influencing the data.

## The quasi-likelihood

The quasi-likelihood method relaxes the variance assumption by including
a `scale`-parameter.

Over-dispersion corresponds to `scale > 1`

Under-dispersion corresponds to `scale < 1`

We can estimate the scale-parameter using the `family = quasi-`
distributions

## If pH was "unknown"...

Assume `pH` was not measured (back to the first model...)

Let's fit a `quasi-poisson` model and look at the estimates. No change!

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
mod1q.glm <- glm(Species ~ Biomass, family=quasipoisson, data=species)
sumfit <- summary(mod1q.glm)
sumfit$coefficients
```

## Quasi-Poisson Output {.smaller}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
mod1q.glm <- glm(Species ~ Biomass, family=quasipoisson, data=species)
summary(mod1q.glm)
```

Compare with the model assuming poisson distribution:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
sumfit1 <- summary(mod1.glm)
sumfit1$coefficients
```

But note the increased standard errors!

## Estimated over/under-dispersion

The estimated dispersion parameter is:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
summary(mod1q.glm)$dispersion
```

The standard errors of the estimated regression coefficients have
increased by a factor of $\sqrt{4.376}= 2.091$

There exist formal tests for over/under-dispersion:

-   Parametric Pearson residuals test

-   Nonparametric Pearson residuals test

-   Simulation-based residual variance test

-   Etc.

## Gamma regression

For continuous variables that are strictly positive and often
right-skewed, we can use the **Gamma distribution**.

Its probability density function is:
$$f(y) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\nu)} \left( \frac{\nu}{\mu} \right)^\nu y^{\nu - 1} \exp\left( - \frac{\nu y}{\mu} \right)$$
for $y > 0$, where $\mu > 0$ is the mean and $\nu > 0$ is the shape
parameter.

The variance of a Gamma distributed variable is proportional to the
square of its mean, $Var(y) = \mu^2 / \nu$, making it ideal when larger
responses have higher variance.

To ensure that the predicted mean $\mu$ is always positive, we typically
use the **log-link**:
$$g(\mu) = \log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{p}$$

## Shapes of the Gamma distribution

The Gamma PDF is highly flexible based on the shape ($\nu$) and mean
($\mu$).

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=6}
y_vals <- seq(0, 15, length.out=200)
plot(y_vals, dgamma(y_vals, shape=1, rate=1/2), type="l", col="red", lwd=2,
     ylab="Density", xlab="y", main="Gamma density for different shape and mean")
lines(y_vals, dgamma(y_vals, shape=2, rate=2/4), col="blue", lwd=2)
lines(y_vals, dgamma(y_vals, shape=5, rate=5/8), col="green3", lwd=2)
legend("topright", legend=c(expression(paste(nu, "=1, ", mu, "=2")), 
                            expression(paste(nu, "=2, ", mu, "=4")), 
                            expression(paste(nu, "=5, ", mu, "=8"))),
       col=c("red", "blue", "green3"), lwd=2)
```

## Gamma regression example

Consider the `Auto` dataset from the `ISLR` package. We want to predict
the continuous and strictly positive `mpg` (miles per gallon) based on
vehicle `weight` and `horsepower`.

```{r, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ISLR)
data(Auto)
head(Auto[, c("mpg", "weight", "horsepower")], 3)
```

## Why not Gaussian?

If we look at the distribution of `mpg`, it is strictly positive and
right-skewed. A standard Gaussian regression assumes symmetric errors
with constant variance, which is not suitable here.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, fig.width=5}
hist(Auto$mpg, breaks=15, main="Histogram of mpg", xlab="mpg", col="lightblue")
```

## Gamma regression fit {.smaller}

```{r, echo=TRUE}
mod.gamma <- glm(mpg ~ weight + horsepower, 
                 family=Gamma(link="log"), data=Auto)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
summary(mod.gamma)
```

## Gamma Interpretation

Both predictors have a significant negative effect on the expected
`mpg`. The variance assumption of the Gamma model naturally handles the
heteroscedasticity common in this type of data.

Because we use the **log-link**, a 1-unit increase in the predictor
$x_j$ multiplies the expected mean response by
$\color{red}{\exp(\beta_j)}$. For instance, since
$\widehat{\beta}_{\text{weight}} = -0.00025$, an increase of 1000 units
in `weight` multiplies the expected `mpg` by
$\color{red}{\exp(-0.25) \approx 0.78}$.

## The Multinomial Distribution

Consider $N$ **independent trials**, each resulting in exactly one of
$t$ **categories** (bins) with fixed probabilities
$\mathbf{p} = (p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_t)$, where $\sum_{j=1}^t p_j = 1$.

Let $Y_j$ = number of trials falling in category $j$. Then the vector
$(Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_t)$ follows a **Multinomial distribution**:

$$\mathbf{Y} \sim \text{Multinomial}(N,\, \mathbf{p})$$

with joint probability mass function:

$$P(Y_1 = k_1, \ldots, Y_t = k_t) = \frac{n!}{k_1!\, k_2!\, \cdots\, k_t!}\; p_1^{k_1}\, p_2^{k_2}\, \cdots\, p_t^{k_t}$$

where $k_1 + k_2 + \cdots + k_t = N$ and for each $j$: $E(Y_j) = N p_j$,
$\quad Var(Y_j) = N p_j (1-p_j)$.

**Note:** When $t=2$ this reduces to the familiar **Binomial**
distribution.

## Multinomial: Bins & Trials Illustration

$n = 20$ trials distributed across $t = 4$ categories:

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=6.5}
set.seed(42)
probs  <- c(0.40, 0.25, 0.20, 0.15)
labels <- c("Cat 1\n[p=0.40]", "Cat 2\n[p=0.25]",
            "Cat 3\n[p=0.20]", "Cat 4\n[p=0.15]")
cols   <- c("#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A", "#FF7F00")
n_trials <- 20
counts <- as.vector(rmultinom(1, size=n_trials, prob=probs))

bp <- barplot(counts, names.arg=labels, col=cols,
              ylim=c(0, max(counts) + 3),
              ylab="Count (number of trials)",
              main=paste0("Multinomial sample: N = ", n_trials,
                          " trials, t = 4 categories"),
              cex.names=0.85)
# overlay expected counts
expected <- n_trials * probs
points(bp, expected, pch=18, cex=1.8, col="black")
segments(bp, expected - 0, bp, expected, lwd=2, col="black")
legend("topright",
       legend=c("Observed counts", "Expected  (N · pj)"),
       fill=c("gray70", NA), pch=c(NA, 18), pt.cex=1.5,
       col=c(NA, "black"), border=c("black", NA), bty="n")
text(bp, counts + 0.8, labels=counts, font=2, cex=1.1)
```

Each bar = one **bin** (category); bar height = how many trials landed
there.

## Categorical Distribution when $N=1$

When we perform only **one trial** ($N = 1$), each $Y_j \in \{0,1\}$ and
exactly one $Y_j = 1$. This is the **Categorical distribution**:

$$Y \sim \text{Categorical}(\mathbf{p}), \quad
P(Y_j = 1) = p_j, \quad j = 1,\ldots,t$$

Think of it as a single **roll of a weighted** $t$-sided die.

**Connection to regression:** In multinomial regression each observation
$i$ is modelled as one Categorical trial with class-probabilities
$p_{ij}$ driven by covariates $\mathbf{x}_i$.

## Example - Iris Species

We want to predict `Species` (setosa, versicolor, virginica) of iris
flowers based on their `Sepal.Length`.

Let $i$ denote a flower, and we have categorical outcome $j=1$ (setosa),
$j=2$ (versicolor), $j=3$ (virginica).

![](images/clipboard-1305837794.png){width="236"}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
data(iris)
head(iris[, c("Sepal.Length", "Species")], 1)
```

## Multinomial model assumptions

Given a flower-specific linear predictor $\eta_{ij}$ for flower $i$ and
species $j$, the probability of outcome $j$ is modelled as:

$$p_{ij} = \frac{\exp(\eta_{ij})}{\sum_k \exp(\eta_{ik})} \text{; known as softmax function}$$

where
$\eta_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1j} \cdot \text{Sepal.Length}_i + \beta_{2j} \cdot \text{Sepal.Width}_i$.

We use baseline response parameterization (default in R) where the first
category (setosa) is the reference, so we set $\eta_{i1} = 0$. This
gives a simplification for $j=1$:

$$p_{i1} = 1 - p_{i2} - p_{i3}$$

## R code (Baseline parameterization) {.smaller}

Let's use the `nnet` package to fit the model.

```{r,echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
MLM.iris <- nnet::multinom(Species ~ Sepal.Length + Sepal.Width,
                            data=iris, trace=FALSE)
summary(MLM.iris)
```

Here `setosa` is the baseline response. The model estimates two sets of
coefficients: one for `versicolor` vs `setosa` and one for `virginica`
vs `setosa`.

## Calculating Probabilities

For a given flower with `Sepal.Length = 6` cm and `Sepal.Width = 3` cm,
the linear predictors are computed from the estimated coefficients
(Remember $\widehat{\eta}_{1} = 0$):

```{r, echo=TRUE}
new_data <- data.frame(Sepal.Length=6, Sepal.Width=3)
round(predict(MLM.iris, newdata=new_data, type="probs"), 4)
```

## Classification Accuracy (Linear Model)

We can evaluate the model's classification accuracy over the entire
dataset:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
predicted_classes <- predict(MLM.iris, newdata=iris, type="class")
accuracy <- mean(predicted_classes == iris$Species)
round(accuracy, 3)
table(Predicted = predicted_classes, Actual = iris$Species)
```

## Linear Decision Boundary in 2D

**Another** model: `Species ~ Sepal.Length + Sepal.Width`.\
Background colours show the predicted class region; points are true
species.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=6.5}
# Build grid
sl_range <- seq(min(iris$Sepal.Length) - 0.2, max(iris$Sepal.Length) + 0.2, length.out=200)
sw_range <- seq(min(iris$Sepal.Width)  - 0.2, max(iris$Sepal.Width)  + 0.2, length.out=200)
grid     <- expand.grid(Sepal.Length = sl_range, Sepal.Width = sw_range)
grid$pred <- predict(MLM.iris, newdata=grid, type="class")

# Pastel region colours
region_cols <- c(setosa="#FFAAAA", versicolor="#AADDAA", virginica="#AAAAFF")
point_cols  <- c(setosa="#CC0000",  versicolor="#006600",  virginica="#0000CC")

image(sl_range, sw_range,
      matrix(as.numeric(factor(grid$pred, levels=levels(iris$Species))),
             nrow=length(sl_range)),
      col=c("#FFAAAA", "#AADDAA", "#AAAAFF"),
      xlab="Sepal Length (cm)", ylab="Sepal Width (cm)",
      main="Linear multinomial: decision boundaries")

points(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width,
       pch=21, bg=point_cols[as.character(iris$Species)], cex=1.1, lwd=0.5)

legend("topright", legend=levels(iris$Species),
       pt.bg=point_cols, pch=21, pt.cex=1.3, bty="n")
```

## Cubic Decision Boundary in 2D

Model: `Species ~ poly(Sepal.Length, 3) + poly(Sepal.Width, 3)`.\
Polynomial terms allow curved, non-linear class boundaries.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=6.5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
MLM.iris.q <- nnet::multinom(
  Species ~ poly(Sepal.Length, 3) + poly(Sepal.Width, 3),
  data=iris, trace=FALSE)

grid$pred_q <- predict(MLM.iris.q, newdata=grid, type="class")

acc_q <- mean(predict(MLM.iris.q, newdata=iris, type="class") == iris$Species)

image(sl_range, sw_range,
      matrix(as.numeric(factor(grid$pred_q, levels=levels(iris$Species))),
             nrow=length(sl_range)),
      col=c("#FFAAAA", "#AADDAA", "#AAAAFF"),
      xlab="Sepal Length (cm)", ylab="Sepal Width (cm)",
      main=paste0("Quadratic multinomial: decision boundaries  (accuracy = ",
                  round(acc_q, 3), ")"))

points(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width,
       pch=21, bg=point_cols[as.character(iris$Species)], cex=1.1, lwd=0.5)

legend("topright", legend=levels(iris$Species),
       pt.bg=point_cols, pch=21, pt.cex=1.3, bty="n")
```
